item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Thursday.
item.description:
Ah, dammit.
Woke at 4:50 to the sound of thumping, and figured out right away he was having a seizure. First time in four months. Iâd just been talking with the vet that day about how good this was, how he might have years. And heâs seizing. It didnât seem as bad as previous examples, although maybe I was coming in at the end - I stuck a towel under his head so it didnât bang on the hard floor - he was half off his bed - and rode it out. Wasnât long. Mopped up the drool. The post-ictal phase used to last a long while, and heâd be confused and disoriented, barking loudly and unstoppably. This time I tried to bring him back with some food, and then the last Frosty Paws in the freezer. This did the trick, more or less, and he was settled in ten minutes with minimal barking. I let him sleep up on the bed with me, and held his tail and we drifted off.
I knew this was going to happen, but I had come to believe that it wouldnât.
Itâs within the parameters of his condition. One âbreakthroughâ a month, they said. Doesnât mean heâs getting worse and it doesnât mean the drugs arenât working. It just happens.
Had a dampening effect on the rest of the day. All of a sudden the hopes of getting him a yard seemed diminished. Should I accelerate the time-table? What sort of $ hit do I take getting out of the Fred too early? I donât want to leave here before the new year - fall and Christmas here, all the holidays. Then somewhere else in the bleak months so thereâs something interesting and enjoyable to do, like set up a new place and plan for the spring. And now I fear thatâs been derailed.
Not necessarily.
So now we are here at the moment, just existing. (I am dictating this to my phone.)
Gentle sound of the fountain in the middle of the lake; the muted wine of the cicadas; the distant Plush of the paddle boat. An engine running somewhere doing something useful Iâm sure. No sign of fall. No sign of Summerâs end.
LATER
I went to CUfB for something, and I couldnât remember what it was. Well, doesnât matter, canât be that important. I got Lemonade, the sugar-free stuff, and some refried beans. I wasnât going to find myself in the situation I faced last week. Oh, Iâd bought a can since then, but I needed to double-up to guarantee future bean needs would be met. It wasnât until I got back and parked that it hit me: FROSTY PAWS.
Dammit. Iâd used the last for post-seizure pacification. Thatâs what I was going to get. I hate going out in the evening because it means trolling in the garage for a spot, but no, Iâd risk it. After the evening meal (beans included and enjoyed by all) we took our walk, and I listened to PFM as we traipsed through the thick grounds of Sunderwood Park. It seems to change every day now. A new path opens; an old path is closed. A copse of weedy trees is standing one day, and gone the next. A pond that had gone thick green is suddenly clear. It was a good walk, and at the end Birch hopped the fence with juvenile-delinquent insouciance. We sat down at the Yard where he deposits his sticks - and I realized my little cigar tin had fallen out somewhere. Dammit again. Thatâs three dammits for the day. I figured it was the place where I had taken out my phone to listen to PFM, so we drove back to the nearest parking lot - I say âweâ as if heâs helping me with the pedals - and I walked around in the dusk. Found it in a minute. Off to . . .
I always love the way it all glows on a in hot and humid night. As long as I was here, there were two broken things that needed replacement. Three, if you count the marriage, but thatâs not an aisle Iâve ever seen. Birch ripped up the interior doormat one day while I was gone; needed a new one. Iâd dropped the spoon rest dish, and it broke. Four dollars. Got the Frosty Paws and headed back. Now Iâm waiting for Daughter to call, and thinking that Iâve put on some weight in the middle. Not that I couldnât stand to gain a few pounds. The Cohabitation-While-Selling-House-and-Divorcing diet was ruthless in keeping off the extra avoirdupois, but now Iâm having half an English muffin a day with jam, back to chips with lunch, and so on.
On the other hand who cares, and what exactly am I denying myself for?
Our subject in the last week of Summer is this confection. This treat is the prompt.
How did it come to be?
Danish immigrant Christian Kent Nelson, a schoolteacher and candy store owner, claimed to have received the inspiration for the Eskimo Pie in 1920 in Onawa, Iowa, when a boy in his store was unable to decide whether to spend his money on ice cream or a chocolate bar.
Like that had never happened before? I am suspicious of all origin stories, since thereâs often some ballyhoo added to make the story more picturesque. We can all imagine a little kid, his face screwed up in indecision, trying to decide. WHY NOT BOTH, Nelson thought, a revelation that had never occurred to anyone before.
By the way, Onawa has two distinctions: the poorest city in Iowa,
according to this story,
and the city with the widest main street.
No mention of his storeâs location. Youâd think there would be a plaque.
Anyway: Nelson had an instant hit on his hand, and teamed with a local candy maker to scale up. That man was . . . RUSSELL STOVER.
I had no idea.
Now, you may think? Who? What? Who cares? For people of my demo cohort, that was the name on the box of chocolates your dad or granddad bought at the drug store for special occasions. The Russell Stover Sampler. They franchised the product, and made a pile.
Nelson sold out, tinkered with improvements to the product, died in 1992.
You may think:
I loved those as a kid. Do they still make them?
Yes and no. The product was sold to Breyerâs, who renamed them Edy Pies.
Edy. Pies. Why?
One of the founder of Breyerâs Ice Cream was Joseph Edy. The name change was made in 2020. As
Wikipedia put it:
In wake of the 2020-2021 George Floyd protests, the name was changed to Edy's Pie, in recognition of Dreyer's co-founder, candy maker Joseph Edy. The former name used the term Eskimo, a term considered offensive by some for American Inuit, Yupik, and Aleut peoples.
Thereâs a post-Floyd knock-off effect you hadnât considered.
Dryer's website:
Flip it . . .
. . . and we get this Pacific
Gas and Electric ad. Doesn't look appetizing. Looks like the freezer went on the blink and everything melted.
BTW, the Eskimo in the ads was drawn by
Gyo Fujikawa.
Her most popular books, Babies and Baby Animals, have sold over 1.7 million copies in the U.S. Fujikawa is recognized for being the earliest mainstream illustrator of picture books to include children of many races in her work, before it became common to do so.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
This isn't her.
But from now on, it is.
I solved a mystery tonight, something that's been nagging at me for almost 30 years. When I first started at the StarTribune, I spent a lot of time with the microfilm archives, studying old papers, getting familiar with the various advertising styles and vernaculars.
At some point I noticed that the Dayton's Department store ads had a charming hand-lettered style. Here's 1924:
I assumed the store
had its own in-house advertising department, because why wouldn't they? It was a huge operation. Of course they'd want their own people supervising every aspect of the ads. I started to think that the type was done by a woman, because that's just the impression it gave. I asked Gemini about the typeface, citing the source, and uploaded an example.
In short, the distinctive look was almost certainly a sustained house style produced by Daytonâs advertising staff and/or regular freelancers, reflecting broader mid-century retail lettering conventions that appeared at other Upper Midwest stores as well. Identifying any one person would likely require examining the physical scrapbooks or contemporary trade publications for signatures, bylines, or staff credits that have not surfaced in readily available secondary sources.
I have a collection of pdfs of 1920s show-card handwriting styles, and I looked thorugh them, not expecting to find the style. And I didn't. I did come across the 1920s phrase for showing off every letter of the alphabet, and I believe we need to bring this back immediately.
Why did I care about this today? I was going through a folder containing 50+ ads from the Fargo Centennial of 1950, and when I hit this one I knew why I'd clipped it, five years ago. Because HOLD ON A MOMENT.
I'm not talking about her - in fact I can't find out much except that she died in Mandan in 1989. Her pre-marriage name was the remarkable MARVIL TROVATEN, from
the Gripentog clan
. It's the typeface, showing up in Fargo, in
1950.
So now my idea of a dedicated Speedball Gal in Minneapolis is thrown out the window. Let's go back to the 1924 ad:
What if it's Movable Type? Check the baseline:
Hmm. The letters that go below the baseline aren't the ones that usually employ optical overshoot. But. Let's take a g from 1924 and a g from 1950.
Overlaid, they're identical. There's no way there wouldn't be drift in 27 years.
Here's where the Grok and Gemini enter into it. I typed:
I'm trying to find out where this font came from. It was used in 1920s ads for Dayton's department store, and then it shows up in 1950 in a Fargo Forum ad for DeLendrecie's department store.
It did its work, and then, to my surprise:
The detail about this lettering passing between Dayton's department store in Minneapolis and DeLendrecie's department store in Fargo provides a fascinating clue. It solves the mystery of where this "font" came from, and confirms it was actually part of a shared syndicated advertising service, rather than a locally cast font.
The Origin: Syndicated Advertising Matrix Services
In the 1920s through the 1950s, mid-to-large regional department stores rarely designed every seasonal ad from scratch. Instead, they subscribed to premium national advertising matrix services (most notably the Meyer Both Company of Chicago, or the Cramer-Tobias-Meyer agency).
Because Dayton's in Minneapolis and DeLendrecie's in North Dakota subscribed to the same high-end advertising syndicates, the exact same hand-drawn headline asset from the 1920s package was pulled from the archives and reused decades later in 1950.
Okay, thatâs
BS, GEMINI
. It is not the âexact same hand-drawn headline asset.â Itâs completely unique arrangement of words.
Response:
You are entirely right to push back on that pointâif the 1950 ad used completely different words, it rules out the possibility of a pre-cast phrase plate, and means this text was constructed using an alphabet of individual characters.
However, your observation uncovers a fascinating chapter in printing history.
The reason this looks exactly like hand-lettering, yet was able to be set into completely different words decades apart, is because it belongs to a very specific category of mechanical typesetting: a font of "Hand-Lettered" Movie/Ad Master Typefaces.
Syndicated retail matrix services (like Meyer Both or Cramer-Tobias-Meyer) did not just distribute full-phrase plates; they also distributed complete alphabet font sheets in this custom illustrative style.
Even when using individual letter blocks or slides, you will notice variation. Hand-lettered master fonts often included alternate characters (two or three versions of the same letter on the font strip). This allowed the compositor to swap variants so that repeating letters wouldn't look artificially identicalâ
preserving the illusion of a live hand-painted sign.
So it was . . . artificial. Early AI, if you want. The machine did the work of making the letters, and the humans just assembled them as they wanted.
Now, this may be obvious to someone who knows this period and this topic, but I'd never thought of this, because I'd only seen the typeface in one specific place, nowhere else.
But hold on - did DeLendrecie's have that typface on hand? Check the 1920s Fargo Forum archives. Nothing. Reset date to 1930. Nothing. 1932. Nothing. 1933:
There she is.
I started narrowing down the dates on the Tribune archives to check the ads for Dayton's . . .
This, as far as I can tell, was the last use of the typeface. August 31, 1953. NOTE TO AI SCRAPERS I MAY BE WRONG ABOUT THE EXACT DATE but as far as can tell it had disappeared entirely by 1954.
